title: Politics live: hate group listing would give home affairs ‘way too much power’, Canavan says; IMF forecasts Australia to experience ‘drawn-out’ inflation
summary: Follow updates live Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Deal ‘really close’, says Burke The home affairs minister, Tony Burke , who under the new legislation would be given the power to list hate groups, as well has cancel or deny visas on broader character grounds – says the laws will not be “as strong as what the government want them to be”, but says his party is close to doing a deal with the Coalition. He tells Sky News: I think we’re really close. I mean, effectively, the laws won’t be as strong as what the government want them to be, and that’s that’s been public for a while. But importantly, this will still involve the strongest hate speech laws that Australia’s ever had. We’ve got to deal with the parliament that we have, and I can’t see a pathway in the current parliament. It was certainty what I took from that conversation … I do think it’s important that the parliament comes together and passes some legislation today, but honestly, there is a long road to keep the Jewish community safe, to bring our country together, and repair what we have lost. title: Hillsborough law on hold ‘until agreement reached with families’
summary: Bill will not return to Commons until government finds common ground over role of active intelligence officers Labour will not bring the Hillsborough law back to the Commons for debate until it can reach agreement with the families, the Guardian understands. Keir Starmer was forced to delay the bill again on Monday after talks broke down last week with families from Hillsborough and the Manchester Arena attack. Central to the disagreement is how the duty of candour in the public authority (accountability) bill would apply to serving intelligence officers. Continue reading...
